paras: The Haile gold mine manhunt was the pursuit of Charles Lloyd, a Black mine worker, by a posse of white men in Lancaster County, South Carolina, in late August 1895, after he was accused of shooting two white youths, killing W. B. Welsh and wounding John Hough. The pursuers were said to be bent on lynching him, but he was captured, wounded, near Monroe, North Carolina, and jailed there. A widely reprinted wire story attributed to Lloyd a declaration that it was time for Black people to kill white men, a claim the local South Carolina reports did not repeat.

Lloyd, called Charlie Loyd in the South Carolina papers, was described as 'a negro employed at the mine' at the Haile gold mine near Kershaw. Welsh, about seventeen, was the son of Capt. J. V. Welsh, and Hough was his companion of the same age; the wire said both came from 'prominent families'.

According to a Kershaw dispatch to The State dated August 25, the shooting took place at about 11 o'clock the previous night, Saturday, August 24. That report said Loyd shot Welsh in the left side and then, as Welsh lay 'begging Loyd not to shoot again', fired through his temple with a .38-calibre pistol, and that a shot from the same pistol broke Hough's right arm.

Loyd escaped, and the Kershaw dispatch reported that 'a posse is in pursuit and if caught he will surely be lynched'. The Columbia special carried by wire to Chicago said he had taken to the mountains with 'a company of white men' after him 'with the avowed purpose of lynching him'. On August 26 he was captured fifteen miles above Monroe, North Carolina, having been 'wounded pretty severely before he gave up'; the dispatch did not say who shot him.

An inquest on Welsh, held on August 25, found 'absolutely no provocation' for the killing. A News and Courier special of August 27 said Loyd had confessed, blamed whiskey for 'the trouble', was held in the Monroe jail and would probably be brought to Lancaster the next day.

The Lancaster Era wrote that the people of Lancaster were 'much wrought up' and that Loyd would have met 'no mercy at the hands of the people' had he been caught there. No report of his transfer to Lancaster, a trial or a sentence appears in the coverage, and no attempt on his life after capture is reported.

Outside South Carolina the story ran as a short wire item dated Columbia, August 26, which several papers printed the same day. The Topeka State Journal headed it 'A Negro Shoots Two White Boys Without Cause', calling Lloyd 'a negro desperado' and 'the brute', while the Wilmington Daily Republican and the Shenandoah Evening Herald used 'Shot by a Negro Desperado'. The Salt Lake Herald put it under the headline 'Lynching Too Good', and the Scranton Tribune reduced it to one line built on the quotation 'It's time to kill white men'.

The wire's account of a racial declaration appears in none of the South Carolina reports, which instead stressed the inquest's finding of no provocation and, later, Loyd's reported statement about whiskey. The local papers treated the threatened lynching as expected and the anger behind it as justified: The Watchman and Southron's headline was 'Cruelly Murdered', it called Loyd 'the fiend', and it said the citizens were 'justly aroused'. The Southern Christian Advocate listed the killing in its weekly news summary as the murder of Welsh 'by Charlie Loyd, colored'. No coverage of the case was found in the Black press.

Only the wire version, from an unnamed Columbia source, says Lloyd announced it was time for Black people 'to begin to kill white men'; the local Kershaw reports mention no such statement. The wire's 'last night' in a dispatch dated August 26 points to August 25, but the Kershaw reports and the Southern Christian Advocate place the shooting on Saturday night, August 24, and the local dispatches are the closer source.

framing.detail: The local special called Welsh 'foully murdered', Loyd 'the fiend', and said citizens were 'justly aroused' while forecasting a lynching.
The Columbia wire, headed 'A Negro Shoots Two White Boys Without Cause' and 'Time to Kill Whites', called Lloyd a 'negro desperado' and 'the brute' and reported the lynching aim without comment.
The Salt Lake Herald headed the wire 'Lynching Too Good'.
